excerpt: What SCDOT, SCDPS and NHTSA crash data show about motorcycle collisions on Dorchester Road, the left-turn crash pattern, and what families can recover.
keyTakeaways: Dorchester Road (SC 642), from North Charleston into Dorchester County, is a hazardous corridor for motorcyclists. In 45% of fatal two-vehicle motorcycle crashes nationally, the other vehicle was turning left (NHTSA, 2024 data). Heavy vehicles, limited sight lines and high speeds reduce survival odds. South Carolina does not require helmets for riders 21 and older (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). Riders can recover damages if less than 51% at fault. The 3-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) governs most injury claims.

faqs.question: Why is Dorchester Road so dangerous for motorcyclists?
faqs.answer: It combines high speeds, heavy truck traffic and unprotected left-turn intersections. Cement mixers, dump trucks and construction vehicles share the corridor. SCDOT counted 17 fatal crashes and 924 injury crashes between the Dorchester County line and Kent Avenue from 2018 through 2022, and in 2024 Dorchester Road was Dorchester County's highest-crash road (SCDPS).

faqs.question: What is the left-turn problem in motorcycle crashes?
faqs.answer: Nationally, in 45% of fatal crashes between a motorcycle and one other vehicle, the other vehicle was turning left (NHTSA, 2024 data). NHTSA reports the crash configuration, not who was at fault. In a typical case, a driver scans oncoming traffic, fails to register the motorcycle's smaller visual profile, judges it as farther away, and turns directly into its path.

faqs.question: How much time does a rider have to react?
faqs.answer: Very little. At 50 mph a motorcycle covers about 73 feet every second, so a vehicle that turns across its path a few car lengths ahead leaves almost no room to stop. That is why these collisions are so often fatal even when the rider does everything right.

faqs.question: Does not wearing a helmet affect my claim in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina law requires motorcycle operators and passengers under age 21 to wear an approved helmet (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). State law does not impose that helmet requirement on riders age 21 or older. For riders 21 and older, the South Carolina Supreme Court has held that riding without a helmet is not contributory negligence or assumption of risk (Mayes v. Paxton, 313 S.C. 109 (1993)). A rider under 21 had a statutory duty, so talk with an attorney about how that affects the claim.

faqs.question: What should a family do after a fatal motorcycle crash on Dorchester Road?
faqs.answer: Act before the scene evidence is gone. Signal timing data, vehicle event data and independent witnesses all become harder to obtain quickly, and a lawyer can preserve them while the family deals with everything else.
